newsitem.title: UK: British experts offer AIDS treatment guidelines.
newsitem.headline: British experts offer AIDS treatment guidelines.

text.p: Britain's top AIDS experts published their guidelines for treating the HIV virus on Friday, saying many doctors were probably confused by the flurry of recent studies and numerous drugs available.

They said AIDS should be treated as soon as symptoms start, but no sooner, that at least two different drugs should be used, and that the combination should be switched as soon as there was evidence it was not working.
The aim of treatment should be suppressing the virus to low levels in the blood, they added.
AIDS therapy has been transformed in the past year by news that cocktails of drugs can work well against the virus -- in some cases knocking it back to undetectable levels.
But there is still no clear direction on which drugs work best, and when they should be given.

Dr Brian Gazzard and Dr Graeme Moyle of London's Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, along with a team of top AIDS specialists from around the country, published their guidelines in the Lancet medical journal on Friday.
There was so much evidence from trials that it could be confusing, they said.

"For most infections treatment begins as soon as practicable after diagnosis but this model may not hold true for HIV infection," they wrote. This was because HIV can stay latent for years, it was not known whether drugs could completely eradicate it and long-term effects of the drugs were not known.
The virus often became resistant to drugs and there was always a question of whether early treatment erased the possibility of later treatment, when illness got really bad.
"We have tried to emphasise the importance of maintaining future treatment options," Moyle said in a telephone interview.
"One needs to consider what one is going to use second up and third up. Even though there is a relatively long list of drugs compared to a few years ago, one can burn through them quickly."
That is because the virus can become resistant to some drugs, and using some can bring on resistance to others.
The guidelines are as follows:
-- Treatment should be offered before substantial deficiency in the immune system ensues
-- Initial treatment should include combinations of at least two drugs
-- Switches in therapy should involve substitution or addition of at least two drugs
-- Measurements of the concentration of HIV (viral load) and CD4 (a molecule involved in immunity) in the blood are essential

-- Reduction in viral load to below that which can be detected by sensitive tests represents the optimal treatment response. Failure to achieve or sustain this control of virus should prompt consideration of therapy modification. This response seems to be achieved most reliably with various combinations of drugs
Studies are now underway or being planned on whether using four drugs works better than using three, and comparing the efficacy of using two, three or four drugs.

Moyle said it might now be better for AIDS to be left to experts to treat. "The expansion of knowledge over the last year or two has really made it difficult for a person who is 'dabbling' in HIV to keep up," he said.
